title: Black Friday marketplace
like: the biggest sale day of an online marketplace like Amazon
brief: Once a year a marketplace puts thousands of deals live at the same minute. Millions browse and search, a few doorbuster items get hammered, and a smaller crowd checks out. A payment must never be taken twice, and the day must survive the card processor having a bad hour.

clarify.q: Can search results and product pages be a little old?
clarify.a: Yes, by a minute. A changed price is checked again at checkout.

clarify.q: Can a shopper be charged twice?
clarify.a: Never. Phones retry when the network is slow, so every payment needs one unique key.

clarify.q: What if the card processor is down?
clarify.a: Orders must still be accepted and paid when it returns. A shopper should see "order received", not an error.
No. A handful of doorbusters take a large share of the taps and the stock counts.

notes: Use the peak and mix to estimate payment and search rates separately.
The card processor is paid from revenue and is not in this budget.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Share of taps on the top doorbusters
numbers.how: A few dozen deals draw most of the crowd, so a few keys are very hot (approx.)

hints: Four different jobs share one site: browsing, searching, the cart and paying. Do they need the same kind of storage?
Serve browsing from a CDN and cache, searching from a search index, carts from a key-value store. Payments go through a queue with one key each.
A queue does not remove a dependency quota or make deadlines disappear. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Split the traffic by what it needs. A CDN and a cache take the browsing and the hot doorbuster pages, a search index answers searches, carts live in a fast key-value store, and orders go to SQL. Payments wait in a queue, carry one key each and reach the processor through a circuit breaker, so a bad hour at the processor costs delay, not orders.

designs.name: Browse from cache, search from an index, pay through a queue
designs.why: Each kind of request gets the store that suits it. The queue and the idempotency store make a retry harmless, and the breaker keeps a failing processor from pulling the shop down with it.

tradeoffs: A cache and CDN make browsing cheap and fast, but a price or a stock count can be a minute old.
A queue in front of payments keeps the site up when the processor is slow, but the final "paid" message arrives later.
One unique key per payment makes a retry safe, at the price of one more lookup on every payment.
A search index is quick but is a second copy of the catalog, so it can lag behind a price change.
editorial.realWorld: Marketplaces can see several times their normal traffic in the first minutes of a sale day. A few doorbuster items take a large share of the taps, and card processors are often rate limited or slow during the biggest hours (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Black Friday marketplace: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Protect hot inventory and keep checkout recoverable during payment failure. Read scaling and inventory correctness are separate responsibilities. Unknown provider outcomes must not become double charges. A queue does not remove a dependency quota or make deadlines disappear.

fields.label: Step 1. A doorbuster attracts most reads. What can be cached?
options: Product views with bounded freshness; reserve stock authoritatively
A cached positive stock value as permission to sell
fields.explanation: Read scaling and inventory correctness are separate responsibilities.

fields.label: Step 2. Checkout retries after a slow processor accepted payment. What key is used?
options: The same order payment key with reconciliation
A fresh key to avoid a stuck payment
fields.explanation: Unknown provider outcomes must not become double charges.

fields.label: Step 3. The processor is down for an hour. What limits queued orders?
options: Explicit reservation expiry, bounded backlog and user-visible pending or refusal states
fields.explanation: A queue does not remove a dependency quota or make deadlines disappear.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 5000 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $17466. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
